record.paper_title: Unfolding the Labyrinth: Open Problems in Physics, Mathematics, Astrophysics and Other Areas of Science
record.original_question: What are the correct answers to the celestial-mechanics problems gathered in this chapter, including whether anything can exceed the speed of light once already moving near light speed, whether a mechanically feasible bridge between planets could exist under realistic gravitational and orbital constraints, how a split planet would evolve under self-gravity, why Earth and Moon are each seen 'above' from fixed surface points on the other body, and how objects, elevators, fluids, and Coriolis effects would behave in tunnels passing through or near the center of the Earth?

evidence.quote: 3.1 Some open problems in Celestial Mechanics
Is it possible to accelerate a photon (or another particle travelling at say 0.99 c), and thus to achieve a speed greater than c?
If one drops an object in the tunnel, will the object stop at the Centre of the Earth or will it oscillate like a pendulum across the centre

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the following collection of idealized celestial-mechanics and classical-mechanics thought experiments, and provide rigorous answers (with proofs or quantitative analyses) to each.

1. (Relativistic speed limit.) Within the framework of special relativity, suppose a massive particle is already travelling at speed 0.99 c in an inertial frame, where c is the speed of light in vacuum. Show whether it is possible, by application of any finite sequence of accelerations, to make its speed in that frame exceed c. Treat also the case of a photon: can a photon be further accelerated to a speed exceeding c?

2. (Bridge between planets.) Two spherical planets of given masses M₁, M₂ and radii R₁, R₂ orbit their common centre of mass on a Keplerian orbit. Determine necessary conditions (in terms of the orbital parameters, tidal forces, material tensile strength, and the rotational states of the planets) for a rigid mechanical bridge connecting fixed surface points on the two bodies to remain in static equilibrium, or prove that no such bridge can exist.

3. (Split planet.) A spherical, self-gravitating planet of uniform density ρ and radius R is instantaneously cut into two equal hemispheres separated by a small gap. Assuming only Newtonian self-gravity and rigid hemispheres, describe the subsequent dynamical evolution: do the hemispheres reunite, oscillate, or separate, and on what time scale?

4. (Mutual visibility of Earth and Moon.) Model the Earth–Moon system as two rigid spheres in synchronous-locked or freely rotating motion. Explain rigorously why, for an observer fixed on the surface of one body at a point from which the other body is visible, the other body always appears "above" the local horizon, and characterize precisely the set of surface points where this holds.

5. (Tunnel through the Earth.) Model the Earth as a sphere of radius R with spherically symmetric mass distribution (consider both the uniform-density case and a realistic radial density profile). 
   (a) An object of mass m is dropped from rest at one end of a straight tunnel passing through the centre. Neglecting friction and air resistance, determine whether the object comes to rest at the centre or executes periodic oscillation; compute the period in the uniform-density case.
   (b) Repeat (a) for a straight tunnel that is a chord not passing through the centre.
   (c) Analyze the behaviour of an incompressible fluid filling such a tunnel.
   (d) Taking the Earth's rotation into account, compute the Coriolis deflection experienced by an object falling through a polar tunnel and through an equatorial tunnel, and discuss the stability of an elevator constrained to the tunnel axis.

Provide complete derivations for each part.
artifact.status_search_result: The collection consists of informal thought experiments compiled as "open problems"; standard classical results address several parts (e.g., relativistic speed limit, simple-harmonic motion through a uniform-density Earth tunnel with period ≈84 min), while others (bridge feasibility, split-planet dynamics) are not formally posed problems with a definitive published resolution. No single authoritative source resolves all parts as a unit, so the overall status is unknown.

status_evidence.title: Gravity train
status_evidence.snippet: For a uniform-density Earth, an object dropped through a tunnel through the centre undergoes simple harmonic motion with period about 84 minutes.
status_evidence.claim: The tunnel-through-Earth sub-question has a standard textbook resolution.

status_evidence.title: Special relativity – speed limit
status_evidence.snippet: No massive particle can be accelerated to the speed of light; photons always travel at c in vacuum.
status_evidence.claim: The relativistic part is settled by standard special relativity.
